definition: DeepSeek is a family of large language models known for an unusual design choice: at any moment, only a small fraction of the model is actually working. It's the difference between calling in two specialists versus assembling the entire hospital for every question — similar answers, far less effort.

panels.annotation: Token-burn note: vagueness multiplies cost. A vague prompt forces more guessing — more reasoning tokens, longer output, more decode laps. “Summarize the pricing section in 5 bullets” can cost a tenth of “summarize this??” for a better answer.

example.body: DeepSeek reported its final training run cost about $5.5 million — startlingly cheap next to competitors' nine-figure runs. The honest caveat: that figure covers the final run only, not the years of research, failed experiments, and engineering that made it possible. It's the cost of the last lap, not the whole race.
example.title: The $5.5M headline

footnotes.body: DeepSeek-V3 uses a Mixture-of-Experts architecture (hundreds of routed experts, only a handful active per token — roughly 5% of parameters active), Multi-head Latent Attention (MLA) which compresses the KV cache for cheaper long-context inference, and auxiliary-loss-free load balancing. The $5.5M figure refers to the final pre-training run's GPU cost.
footnotes.label: For the technical reader

footnotes.body: Expert counts and active-parameter ratios vary across DeepSeek versions; treat “~5%” as illustrative of sparse activation, not a spec-sheet value. Training-cost figures exclude prior R&D, data, and staff.
footnotes.label: Caveats on the numbers

name: DeepSeek
tagline: The famously efficient open model — a case study in doing more with fewer active parameters.
whyItMatters: DeepSeek made “efficient AI” concrete for the public: you don't always need the biggest, most expensive model running at full power. Its design is also a perfect window into what's actually inside a modern AI model.
